doc_name: List of Tom and Jerry characters
text: The Tom and Jerry animated series features a list of characters introduced in chronological order. Thomas "Tom" (originally named "Jasper") is a bluish grey and white domestic shorthair cat, typically living a comfortable, pampered life, while Gerald "Jerry" (originally called "Jinx"), a brown house mouse, lives nearby. Despite being larger and more energetic, Tom is no match for Jerry’s intelligence and strength, often able to lift heavy objects like anvils and withstand significant impacts. Though cats usually chase mice to eat them, Tom rarely attempts to eat Jerry; instead, he often taunts him or seeks rewards from humans for catching him. Jerry usually wins by the end of each cartoon, though Tom triumphs occasionally—such as in The Million Dollar Cat, where Jerry’s actions provoke Tom’s retaliation, or in Timid Tabby, where Tom’s cousin pushes Jerry too far. Rarely, both characters lose, like in Filet Meow, where Jerry’s trap backfires, or when Jerry overlooks something. They occasionally form temporary truces, such as in Posse Cat, where they agree to share a reward, but these break down when one reneges. In Snowbody Loves Me, they end on a friendly note. Both characters exhibit sadistic tendencies, enjoying tormenting each other, but show conscience when one is in danger from an unplanned event or a third party. They sometimes bond over shared negative experiences and act as allies against third-party tormentors, though these alliances dissolve when unexpected events occur or when one feels the other is no longer needed. Characters introduced in the theatrical shorts directed by William Hanna and Joseph Barbera include Spike, a stern, occasionally dim-witted grey bulldog who disapproves of cats but is gentle toward mice, with a possessiveness over his bone and ticklishness; Spike’s first speaking role was in The Bodyguard (1944), voiced initially by Billy Bletcher until 1949, and later by others including Patrick McGeehan, Jerry Mann, Bob Shamrock, John Brown, Fred Karbo, Stan Freberg, and Daws Butler; Spike is protective of his son Tyke, who does not speak in Tom and Jerry or the 2014 TV series (except for laughing in one short), but speaks in Tom and Jerry Kids, voiced by Patric Zimmerman. Nibbles (also known as Tuffy) is a small blue/gray, diaper-wearing orphan mouse who appears frequently with Jerry, especially in comics; his debut was in The Milky Waif (1946), and he was featured in the Academy Award-winning short The Little Orphan (1949); he is sometimes called Jerry’s nephew but is more accurately described as an orphan; he is often shown eating excessively and was left on Jerry’s doorstep in his first appearance; Tom chases him as much as Jerry. Though created as Tuffy in comics in 1942, early animated appearances used the name Nibbles; from the 1950s onward, he was called Tuffy on-screen; in Tom and Jerry: The Magic Ring (2002), he is named Nibbles again and is portrayed as a pet-store mouse unknown to Jerry. In Mouseketeer shorts, Nibbles speaks in French and English, and is not Jerry’s nephew but the son of François Mouse, whose name appears in Touché, Pussy Cat! (1954); he is often mistaken for a girl due to his high-pitched voice, voiced by Francoise Brun-Cottan, Lucille Bliss, Lou Scheimer, Frank Welker, Charlie Adler, Tara Strong, Reece Thompson, Chantal Strand, Kath Soucie (from 2010), and Alan Marriott (in video games). Butch, a black alley cat, first appeared in Baby Puss (1943) alongside Topsy and Meathead, though unnamed in The Alley Cat (1941), where he was referred to as "Tom" in a model sheet; in Baby Puss, he torments Tom after Tom is dressed up as a baby; he is the leader of alley cat bullies who help Tom catch Jerry and competes with Tom over Toodles Galore, creating a love triangle in Springtime for Thomas (1946) and Casanova Cat (1951); in A Mouse in the House (1947), he battles Tom to catch Jerry; in Blue Cat Blues (1956), he is portrayed as a millionaire; he appears in Scat Cats (1957) as a house cat owned by George and Joan. Butch is voiced by Harry E. Lang in The Alley Cat, Jack Mather in Baby Puss, Frank Graham in Springtime for Thomas and Trap Happy (1946), Raul Martinez in Springtime for Thomas (singing voice), Jerry Mann in Casanova Cat, Fred Karbo in Life with Tom, Daws Butler in Baby Butch (1954), Smarty Cat (1955), and Scat Cats (1957), Alan Marriott in Fists of Furry (2000), Marc Silk in War of the Whiskers (2002), Maurice LaMarche in The Magic Ring (2002), Tony Cervone in The Karate Guard (2005), Colin Murdock in Tom and Jerry Tales (2006–08), Joey D'Auria in The Tom and Jerry Show (2014–2021) and Tom and Jerry in New York (2021), and Nicky Jam in Tom & Jerry (2021). Toodles Galore is an attractive white female cat with a large blue bow, considered Tom’s love interest though Tom is a playboy with other interests; she is the only love interest to appear more than twice; Tom lost her to Butch and Spike, and in Casanova Cat (1951), she fell in love with Jerry. Toodles is one of the more anthropomorphic animals, with human-like features such as sitting in human poses, walking on two feet, having human-shaped hands with painted nails, and human-like eyes and lips; she wears a bathing suit in Salt Water Tabby (1947) and has cat ears and nose; she never speaks and rarely moves. She appears in four episodes of Tom and Jerry Tales (2006–2008): "Joy Riding Jokers," "Spaced Out Cat," "Piranha Be Loved By You," "Abracadumb," and "Flamenco Fiasco," credited as "Senorita Cat" in the latter, voiced by Chantal Strand; in The Tom and Jerry Show (2014–2021), she makes cameo appearances in "Belly Achin'", "Cat Napped," "Don't Cut the Cheese," and "A Star Forlorn," and has a full appearance in Season 4’s "Tap Cat"; she appears in Tom and Jerry in New York, voiced by Rachael MacFarlane; a similar white cat appears in the 2021 film. Mammy Two Shoes (voiced by Lillian Randolph) is an African-American woman whose role as a maid or homeowner is never clarified; her face is never seen except briefly in Saturday Evening Puss (1950), and she usually beats Tom (addressed as "Thomas") with a broom when he misbehaves or tries to get rid of Jerry; she appears in 19 cartoons from Puss Gets the Boot (1940) to Push-Button Kitty (1952); Anita Brown voices her in The Mouse Comes to Dinner; the character became controversial due to the Mammy archetype and was retired in 1953; Gene Deitch avoided her due to its outdated nature; MGM Animation/Visual Arts, under Chuck Jones, replaced her with a rotoscoped white woman (mostly stocky or thin), with Randolph’s voice replaced by June Foray’s Irish-accented or generic young adult voice; three years after Turner acquired the series, Lillian Randolph’s voice was replaced by Thea Vidale, who re-recorded dialogue to remove stereotypes. Little Quacker is a duck and recurring character appearing in Little Quacker (1950), Just Ducky (1953), Downhearted Duckling (1954), Southbound Duckling (1955), That's My Mommy (1955), Happy Go Ducky (1958), and The Vanishing Duck (1958); he speaks frequently, with a "duck voice" similar to Disney’s Donald Duck; he is trusting, even allowing Tom to eat him; he is a friend of Jerry but has no hard feelings toward Tom; in three cartoons, he is separated from his mother at birth and reunites with her in two; in That's My Mommy, he is adopted by Tom; in Little Quacker, his father Henry appears; due to differing birth depictions, he may have siblings; he has a girlfriend named Fifi in Downhearted Duckling; he appears in "The Lost Duckling" (1975) in The Tom and Jerry Show; he inspired Yakky Doodle in Hanna-Barbera shows and Hard Luck Duck in What a Cartoon! (1995), voiced by Russi Taylor. Quacker is voiced by Red Coffey in classic shorts, Don Messick in The Tom and Jerry Show (1975), Alan Marriott in Fists of Furry and War of the Whiskers (named "Duckling" in those games), and Sam Kwasman in The Tom and Jerry Show (2014) and Tom and Jerry in New York. Cuckoo, a canary first appearing in Kitty Foiled (1948), also appears in The Flying Cat (1952), Life with Tom (1953), Hic-cup Pup (1954), Two Little Indians (red version), and Matinee Mouse (reusing clips); he is Jerry’s best friend and can carry heavy objects, such as a bowling ball or a 2000 lb. weight. Lightning, a ginger orange cat, first appears in Old Rockin' Chair Tom (1948) as Tom’s rival, named for his speed; in later appearances, he is one of Tom’s alley cat rivals with the same design as Butch but in orange; in Mucho Mouse, he speaks Spanish and is a house cat; he appears in Switchin' Kitten (Gene Deitch) and Catty-Cornered (Chuck Jones), where he has a more orange-yellow color, black tail and ears; he also appears in the live-action film, voiced by Joey Wells. Topsy is a grey/brown Scottish Fold kitten, one of Tom’s alley cat friends/foes, though in Professor Tom he befriends Jerry; he first appears in Baby Puss and last in Scat Cats; in Tom and Jerry Tales, he has a more yellowish color; in Professor Tom, he is explicitly a house cat; more often, he is an alley cat or of unknown origin; in the live-action film, he is voiced by Harry Ratchford. Meathead is a brown, mangy alley cat with a red toupee, first appearing in Sufferin' Cats! (1943) as Tom’s rival; he appears in Baby Puss and other shorts as a rival or ally; he is known as Frankie in Heavenly Puss; in Scat Cats, his final appearance, he is portrayed with all-gray fur. Meathead appears in several episodes of Tom and Jerry Tales with an orange color similar to Lightning, and has a red nose; in two episodes, he has a bush.

doc_name: List of Tom and Jerry characters
text: Jerry first appears in Baby Puss and makes his final appearance in the original theatrical shorts in Scat Cats. In Tom and Jerry Tales, he is depicted with a more yellowish color, similar to Life with Tom. Topsy, another character, is explicitly a house cat in Professor Tom; more often, he is shown as an alley cat or of unknown origin, as seen in Saturday Evening Puss and other shorts. In the live action film, Topsy is voiced by Harry Ratchford. Meathead is a brown, mangy alley cat who wears a red toupee, occasionally matching the color of his fur; he is generally portrayed as dull-witted and first appears in Sufferin' Cats! (1943) as Tom's rival. He also appears in Baby Puss and other shorts as one of Tom's alley cat buddies or foes, known as Frankie in Heavenly Puss. In Scat Cats, his final appearance, he is portrayed with an all-gray color. Meathead appears in several episodes of Tom and Jerry Tales with an orange color similar to Lightning, has a red nose, and in two episodes, a bushy tail. He reappears in the episode "Cruisin' for a Bruisin'" as a lead antagonist, while a drag version named "Meathelda" appears in "Hop to It!". He makes multiple appearances in later seasons, usually alongside Butch and other alley cats, and appears in the live action film, voiced by Na'im Lynn. George and Joan, voiced by Daws Butler (1954–1957; George), Richard Anderson (1958; George), June Foray (1954–1956; Joan), Julie Bennett (1956–1958; Joan), Pilar Arcos (1957; Joan), and Perry Sheehan (1958; Joan), are an average middle-class white couple who debut in Pet Peeve (1954), replacing Mammy Two Shoes. They own Tom, Jerry, and Spike, though Tom likes to keep Joan company and Spike likes to keep George company. Joan is often seen cooking or sitting on her armchair knitting or sewing a dress with Tom nearby. George hates monthly bills and complains they are too expensive, but when not complaining, he reads the newspaper in his smart purple or grey suit, with Spike keeping him company. Both are kind and polite to each other and to Tom and Spike. In Pet Peeve, they decide to keep Jerry as a pet because he is easy to care for and eats little, telling Tom and Spike to leave. However, in later shorts, Tom and Spike still live with them, and Jerry is not a pet. George and Joan appear in three other shorts: Tom's Photo Finish, Busy Buddies, and The Vanishing Duck (Quacker's last short), and one Spike and Tyke short, Scat Cats. In some shorts, Joan appears without George, such as in Mouse for Sale, The Flying Sorceress, Mucho Mouse, and Tot Watchers, suggesting George is working at his office. Jeannie, the babysitter of George and Joan's baby, is an average teenager who spends much of her time on the phone and is often called upon to look after the baby. She leaps straight onto the phone when George and Joan shut the front door, indicating negligence. Despite this, she is kind, friendly, cheerful, and rarely loses her smile—except when scolding Tom for "bothering the baby," which she believes Tom and Jerry do on purpose. Jeannie and the baby appear in only two cartoons: Busy Buddies (1956) and Tot Watchers (1958). Jeannie is voiced by Janet Waldo in the original shorts; in Tom & Jerry Kids, the babysitter is slightly younger and a redhead instead of a blonde. In Tom and Jerry: The Magic Ring, the baby's name is changed to Freddie and he is hostile toward Jerry (though it could be a different mouse identical to Muscles). Due to modern sensibilities, this negligent climax is no longer used in newer entries because child neglect is now a serious issue. A handful of teenage babysitters in The Flintstones have a similar climax. The Ants are an army of red ants who steal food and appear in Cat Napping, Pup on a Picnic, Barbecue Brawl, and Carmen Get It!, and also in Tom & Jerry Kids. They are unusually heavy for their size, and their combined weight often breaks items like Tom's hammock or causes tables and diving boards to shake. It is unclear how or why they are so heavy. Each guardian devil for Tom and Jerry appears in three cartoons: Sufferin' Cats! (1943), Springtime for Thomas (1946), and Smitten Kitten (1952). In the first, one serves as an evil conscience for Tom and in the other for Jerry. A tiny goldfish lives in the same house as Tom and Jerry and first appears in The Little Goldfish (1939) by Rudolf Ising. Major roles come in Jerry and the Goldfish (1951) and Filet Meow (1966), where Tom's attempts to eat her lead to Jerry winning her affections. She appears in cameo roles in Puss Gets the Boot (1940), Puss n' Toots (1942), Baby Puss (1943), The Million Dollar Cat (1944), Casanova Cat (1951), The Missing Mouse (1953), Haunted Mouse (1965), and The Brothers Carry-Mouse-Off (1965). Muscles is Jerry's cousin and a mouse with incredible strength. In Jerry's Cousin (1951), Muscles appears to hate cats, including Tom. In Haunted Mouse, another mouse named Merlin, also a cousin of Jerry's, appears as a wizard with magical abilities. Muscles appears again in Tom and Jerry: The Magic Ring, where his name is changed to Freddie and he is hostile toward Jerry (though it could be a different mouse identical to Muscles). He is voiced by Paul Frees in Jerry's Cousin and by Billy West in Tom and Jerry: The Magic Ring. He also appears in The Tom and Jerry Show. George is the cat counterpart of Muscles, identical to Tom (though shorter) and a cousin. Unlike Muscles, George is a coward and afraid of mice. He first appears in Jerry's Cousin, where he is thrashed by Muscles (possibly explaining his fear), and has a bigger role in Timid Tabby (1957), where he overcomes his fear. He appears in Tom & Jerry Kids, where his fear seems to reappear even though he pretends it hasn't (his name is changed to Tim in that short). He is voiced by Bill Thompson. Fluff, Muff, and Puff are a trio of brown, black, and orange kittens who first appear in Heavenly Puss (1949) in a cameo during Tom's dream as charming kittens who drown. They also appear as cute but mischievous kittens in Triplet Trouble (1952) and on The Tom and Jerry Show. Chérie is a brown/grey female mouse who serves as Jerry's love interest. She first appears at the end of Springtime for Thomas (1946), then in Smitten Kitten (1952), Touché, Pussy Cat! (1954, where she has an identical twin), Tom and Chérie (1955, the first cartoon where she is named, seen only in silhouette), and The Mouse from H.U.N.G.E.R. (1967, as a ticking time bomb set by Tom). Toots refers to three different characters. The first is a fluffy beige cat in Puss n' Toots (1942) and The Mouse Comes to Dinner (1945), the latter being her only speaking role; she also has a cameo in The Bodyguard (1944) and Smitten Kitten (1952). This version appears in some 1940s Tom and Jerry comics and in The Tom and Jerry Show (2014–2021), mistakenly credited as "Toodles" and voiced by Alicyn Packard. Toots is also a different cat in The Zoot Cat (1944) and in the Tom and Jerry Tales episode "Kitty Cat Blues." She is occasionally and erroneously called "Sheikie," but this is actually Tom's nickname, as seen on a gift card. Finally, Toots is a mouse who serves as Jerry's love interest in Blue Cat Blues (1956). Toots also appears as an antagonist in Love Me, Love My Mouse (1966). In some mouseketeer series, Tom serves as the king of France, a clear reference to Louis XIV, who is shown as extremely short-tempered and cruel. In The Two Mouseketeers (1952), the king executes Tom; in Royal Cat Nap (1958), he orders Tom's execution. Mechano cat first appears in Push Button Kitty (1952) as Tom's rival. Later, Mechano and Robot-Mouse appear as a cat-like-robot and mouse-like-robot who serve Tom and Jerry, except in Advance and Be Mechanized (1967), when they get revenge and switch roles, controlling their minds and making them do the work. Mechano's attempts to catch or trap Jerry or Robot-Mouse always backfire for Tom, except in Advance and Be Mechanized, where he initially succeeds in catching Robot-Mouse. In Guided Mouse-ille, he can stand upright and use hands to operate a gun from a mobile tank, which backfires, leaving him with a black face and crying in frustration. He sneaks back and shoots Tom, who attempts to shoot him back, but the shot comes out on the wrong end, causing Tom to faint, leaving Mechano laughing. He also appears in the Tom and Jerry Tales episode "Tin Cat of Tomorrow" (2006), where he is named Verminator 7000. Mechano (called "Robot Cat") appears as a fighter in the video game War of the Whiskers (2002) and is voiced by Marc Silk. The St. Bernard is a dog who first appears in Puttin' on the Dog (1944) and again in The A-Tom-Inable Snowman (1966). Unlike other dogs, he is not hostile to cats and once becomes Tom's medical aid. He also appears in War Dogs and Little Cesario. Eagle is an eagle that tries to steal Jerry for food from Tom. He first appears in Flirty Birdy, then in The Tom and Jerry Show episode "The Egg and Tom and Jerry" (1975, where he is female), and again in Tom and Jerry Tales episode "Bend it like Thomas" (2007). Eagle also appears as a playable character in War of the Whiskers (2002), voiced by Marc Silk. Lion debuted in Slap Happy Lion (1947) by Tex Avery. He transitions from a tame cat in Jerry and the Lion (1950) to a nervous one in "The Hypochondriac Lion" (1975) to a monster in "You're Lion" (2007). He is a playable character in Tom and Jerry in War of the Whiskers, voiced by Alan Marriott. A baby woodpecker first appears in Hatch Up Your Troubles (1949) and its remake The Egg and Jerry (1956), where he can peck into anything, including Tom's stomach or golf club in Tee for Two (1945). Baby Woodpecker and his Mama make cameo appearances in The Tom and Jerry Show (2014). Uncle Pecos is Jerry's cowboyish uncle who appears in Pecos Pest (1955). He is voiced by Shug Fisher and is known to play guitar, wear a black cowboy hat covering his eyes, and pluck each of Tom's whiskers to replace broken strings. Being from Texas, he is shown as super strong and has a stammer, especially while singing. He returns in the Tom and Jerry Tales episode "Cry Uncle" (2006), voiced by Scott McNeil, where he arrives at Tom and Jerry's house, annoys them with music, and leaves with Auntie Spinner at the end. He makes a second return in The Tom and Jerry Show, voiced by Stephen Stanton, in episodes "I Quit," "Uncle Pecos Rides Again," and "Cat-A-Tonic Mouse" (all 2018). A trio of cats—black, brown, and orange—offer extermination services and first appear in Jerry's Cousin and again in Karate Guard, failing to live up to their promise in each. Butch is the leader in Karate Guard, though he holds that role alone in Trap Happy. A radio with a male human voice broadcasts music, cookery shows, and warnings about escaped animals or bomb threats. In Jerry's Diary (1949), the radio is anthropomorphic (with announcer "Uncle Dudley"), though not in other cartoons. The radio's announcements often cause trouble for Tom, such as in Jerry and the Lion (1950), Little Runaway (1952), The Missing Mouse (1953), Down Beat Bear (1956), fear in Fraidy Cat (1942), embarrassment in Jerry's Diary (1949) and Life with Tom (1953), or as a cause of evil intentions in Jerry and the Goldfish (1951). The radio is voiced by Martha Wentworth in Fraidy Cat, Jerry Mann in The Zoot Cat and Life with Tom, Harry E. Lang in Jerry's Diary, Frank Graham in Jerry and the Lion, Daws Butler in Jerry and the Goldfish and Down Beat Bear, and Paul Frees in The Missing Mouse and Down Beat Bear. Unlike other characters, this is not a character per se but a substitution for another, such as Spike the Bulldog, used for a brief visual gag. A character turns into a jackass when fooled, such as Spike in Solid Serenade (1946), The Framed Cat (1950), and Pet Peeve (1954), or Tom in Polka-Dot Puss (1949). In Pup on a Picnic (1955), 'Jackass' is replaced with 'Sucker'. Characters introduced in the theatrical shorts directed by Gene Deitch in the early 1960s include an overweight, short-tempered, average height, middle-aged, bald white man who becomes Tom's owner in only three of the thirteen cartoons: Down and Outing (1961), High Steaks (1962), and Sorry Safari (1962). Unlike other owners, he has severe anger issues and is repeatedly violent toward Tom. He is voiced by Allen Swift. The Grumpy Owner bears a strong resemblance to Clint Clobber (also voiced by Swift), the property manager of a rundown apartment building created for Terrytoons in the mid to late 1950s. There is debate over whether they are the same character, but Deitch claimed they are different. He is a mad scientist reminiscent of Frankenstein, first appearing in Switchin' Kitten (1961). He is the owner of Jerry (who is also his assistant) and has numerous cats trapped in a prison. When Jerry picks an orange cat named Lightning, the other cats flee in terror as the scientist pulls him out for an experiment. He switches Lightning's mind with that of a bulldog and presents the bulldog as a gift to Jerry. An unnamed thin white lady is Tom's owner in Buddies Thicker Than Water (1962). Chuck Jones uses her in The Unshrinkable Jerry Mouse (1964) and in the revised version of Saturday Evening Puss. She also appears in the movie Tom and Jerry: The Fast and the Furry (2005). Like many early owners, her face is never shown. Characters introduced in theatrical shorts produced by Chuck Jones in the mid to late 1960s include a nameless mouse-sized bulldog designed similarly to Spike the Bulldog, who is Jerry's pet dog companion.

doc_name: List of Tom and Jerry characters
text: The mad scientist, first appearing in a theatrical short, is the owner of Jerry, who also serves as his assistant, and holds numerous cats in a prison; when Jerry selects an orange cat named Lightning, the other cats flee in fear as the scientist pulls him out for an experiment, switching Lightning’s mind with that of a bulldog and presenting the bulldog as a gift to Jerry. An unnamed thin white lady serves as Tom’s owner in Buddies Thicker Than Water (1962), and also appears in The Unshrinkable Jerry Mouse (1964), the revised version of Saturday Evening Puss, and Tom and Jerry: The Fast and the Furry (2005); her face is never shown. In mid to late-1960s theatrical shorts produced by Chuck Jones, a nameless mouse-sized bulldog, designed similarly to Spike, appears in only two shorts—The Cat's Me-Ouch (1965) and Purr-Chance to Dream (1967)—as Jerry’s pet dog companion, defending him against Tom; he is presumed to be the oldest son of Spike before Tyke, with a big bite like the Tasmanian Devil, and shares Spike’s appearance and personality. A shark that attempts to eat Tom and Jerry appears in Puss 'n' Boats and Filet Meow (1966) and Surf-Bored Cat and Cannery Rodent (1967); it is a blue shark in Cannery Rodent and Surf-Bored Cat, and a great white shark in the other two. In the first half of the 1975 season of The Tom and Jerry Show television series, a gopher who eats vegetables appears in Gopher Broke and The Son of Gopher Broke; a parody of Robin Hood and His Merry Men, including the character based on the Robin Hood tales, appears in Robin Ho Ho and Tom and Jerry: Robin Hood and His Merry Mouse (2012); the primary antagonist in both is based on the Robin Hood character; a love interest for both Tom and Jerry appears in The Ski Bunny and The Tennis Menace; a police officer appears in See Dr. Jackal and Hide and in The Police Kitten, where he is the superior officer to both Tom and Jerry. In The Tom and Jerry Comedy Show, a Basset Hound with a miserable expression, originally from Tex Avery’s 1940s shorts, first appears in a poster cameo in Matinee Mouse (1966) during the Chuck Jones era, and appears in Droopy and Dripple segments, Tom and Jerry Kids, and Tom and Jerry Tales, sometimes opposing Spike; an anthropomorphic, sluggish, sleepy bear from Harman-Ising’s 1930s shorts also appears in direct-to-video films. McWolf, initially named "Slick Wolf," is the villain in the Droopy and Dripple segments, a cruel wolf whose mission is to ruin Droopy’s (and Dripple’s) life and sometimes stay with Miss Vavoom in Tom & Jerry Kids; he is based on the wolf in Red Hot Riding Hood and is voiced by Frank Welker. In Tom & Jerry Kids, Dripple is the son of Droopy, an older version of the infant pup from Homesteader Droopy (1954), always with his father and sometimes thinking better than him; his mother is never mentioned, though Droopy’s frequent relationship with Miss Vavoom suggests she may be dead or divorced with no visitation rights; he is voiced by Charlie Adler. The recurring woman of the show is seductive, changes hairdos, is conquered by Droopy, and is often targeted by McWolf; she is based on Red from Red Hot Riding Hood (1943) and voiced by Teresa Ganzel; she is sometimes called Bubbles Vavoom, Ultra Vavoom, or Sugar Vavoom. A gold cat host of a demonstration and participation show, with a rancher accent and sometimes acting as an enemy to Tom, is purportedly inspired by Southern California car dealer Cal Worthington and voiced by Phil Hartman. Urfo, a six-legged alien dog, frequently arrives on Earth to help Jerry fight Tom; his owners often send people to retrieve him. Clyde, a fat cat who causes problems for Tom despite trying to be friendly and helpful, is voiced by Brian Cummings and appears uncredited in the live-action film Butch's gang. A mangy orange cat, first appearing as an antagonist of Spike or Tyke, is voiced by Pat Fraley. A medically challenged yellow swallow, friends with Jerry in Hard to Swallow, changes to blue in "Swallow the Swallow" and "Grab that Bird" due to being chased by Clyde and Kyle, is voiced by David L. Lander. A grayish-green, shaggy fanged mouse who occasionally replaces Jerry and outwits his foes, voiced by Frank Welker, first appears in "Wildmouse" and is last seen in "King Windmouse." A cougar who torments Spike and Tyke, wanting to eat Tyke’s lunch and prevented by Spike, is voiced by Frank Welker. The elderly sheriff of Hokey Finokey Swamp is arrogant, rude, and self-centered, threatening to send Swampy back to the circus, which he knows promotes animal cruelty, and envies the map Swampy made to find hidden treasure; he appears in "Cajun Gumbo" as the main antagonist and also serves as an antagonist with the Gator Brothers in another episode featuring Wild Mouse. The Gator Brothers are Sheriff Potgut’s henchmen and appear in "Cajun Gumbo" and another episode with Wild Mouse. Stinky Jr. is the son of McWolf and shares his father’s personality. Screwball Squirrel, based on the original Screwy Squirrel from 1944, now takes place in a public city park, where he messes with hot-headed park attendant Dweeble and his dumb guard dog Rumpley; he is voiced by Charlie Adler and appears in one direct-to-video film, Tom and Jerry's Giant Adventure, voiced by Paul Reubens, and makes a cameo in the Season 3 episode "Kid Stuff" of The Tom and Jerry Show. A squirrel superhero, flamboyant and campy, who throws lightning bolts and speaks with a slight Minnesotan accent, appears in the spin-off series Droopy, Master Detective and is voiced by Charlie Adler. In Tom and Jerry Tales, Mauricio, a very amorous octopus gentleman first appearing in the 1953 live-action musical film Dangerous When Wet during a Tom and Jerry sequence with Esther Williams, is voiced by Fernando Lamas and later by David Kaye in "Octo Sauve," where he mistakes Tom for a mermaid and wants to date him, leading them to get lost at sea. The princess appears in Medieval Menace, where she kisses Tom, who has turned into a frog, thinking he is a prince transformed by a spell; she is voiced by Nicole Bouma. Mrs. Two Shoes, a white woman with a personality and name similar to Mammy Two Shoes, appears in "Ho, Ho Horrors," where photos on a mantel suggest she has a family (a man and a boy, shown only as legs and partial torsos); she is voiced by Nicole Oliver. In the 2014 television series Tom and Jerry Show, Rick (voiced by Jason Alexander and later Stephen Stanton) and Ginger (voiced by Grey DeLisle) are a middle-class couple; Rick is more sympathetic toward Spike while Ginger favors Tom; their faces are never seen, but their voices are featured. The Hamster is a small, anti-social, overachieving hamster with light brown fur who wears glasses and is the smartest hamster in the lab. Bot is a robot that cleans the lab with a vacuum and control arm, has a red screen that spots trash, and often mistakes Tom for trash. Beatie and Hildie are witch sisters who serve as Tom and Jerry’s medieval owners. The detective, owner of Tom (and presumably Jerry), appears in first-season episodes such as "Feline Fatale," "One of a Kind," "Haunted Mouse," "Sleuth or Consequences," "Poof!," "Bone Dry," "Cat Napped," and "Curse Case Scenario," where Tom and Jerry work as sleuths using his name and fame in his absence. Dr. Bigby is an eccentric scientist whose experiments often go wrong, and is the owner of Jerry, Napoleon, the Hamster, and Bot. Skid, an orange cat who is always the leader and elected Top Cat, competes with both Tom and Butch for the Golden Fez in the Top Mouse Catchers. George and Junior are based on the original George and Junior from Tex Avery’s 1940s shorts and appear in the Season 4 episode "Shadow of a Doubt" of The Tom and Jerry Show. In various Tom and Jerry movies, Robyn Starling is a young girl whose father Tom and Jerry helped her find in Tom and Jerry: The Movie; she is voiced by Anndi McAfee. Biff Buzzard and Buzz Blister appear in Tom and Jerry: Blast Off to Mars and Tom and Jerry: The Fast and the Furry; in the latter, they are news reporters, and in the former, they are astronauts; Biff is voiced by Billy West and Buzz by Jess Harnell. Blue Parrot Betty is a pet parrot owned by Blue Pirate Bob in Tom and Jerry: Shiver Me Whiskers; she is voiced by Kathy Najimy. Tin, Pan, and Alley are a trio of male Siamese cats created for direct-to-video films, serving as secondary antagonists in Tom and Jerry Meet Sherlock Holmes, Tom and Jerry: Robin Hood and His Merry Mouse, Tom and Jerry's Giant Adventure, Tom and Jerry: The Lost Dragon, and Tom and Jerry: Spy Quest, acting as henchmen for main antagonists; in Tom and Jerry Meet Sherlock Holmes, they are local gravediggers for Professor Moriarty; in Tom and Jerry: Robin Hood and His Merry Mouse, they work as spies for Prince John; in Tom and Jerry: The Lost Dragon, they are the Hench-cats of Drizelda; in Tom and Jerry: Spy Quest, they work for Doctor Zin; they also appear in Tom and Jerry: Willy Wonka and the Chocolate Factory; named after the 1943 Warner Bros. short Tin Pan Alley Cats; Tin is voiced by Greg Ellis, Pan by Jess Harnell, and Alley by Richard McGonagle. Butch, originally known as Spike until renamed to avoid confusion with Spike from the Tom and Jerry cartoons, is a bulldog from Tex Avery’s 1940s and 1950s shorts, a main antagonist in Droopy shorts (replaced by Hanna-Barbera’s Spike in the 1980s), and has a series of his own; he appears in movies such as Tom and Jerry and the Wizard of Oz and Tom and Jerry: The Magic Ring.
